prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) NextGen targets National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) integrates ground/aircraft decision aids for efficient weather avoidance, Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), and en route/arrival metering.
Actors/elements: FAA traffic managers, air traffic control system/controllers, aircraft, aircraft/flight operators, airline flight dispatchers, pilots/flight crews, general public, NASA, industry, other air traffic management (ATM) stakeholders, flight management systems, onboard weather radar.
Existing operations: TMIs divert aircraft around weather and meter demand to safe-separation capacity. Managers designate forecast convection regions as Flow Constrained Area (FCA); Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), alias Playbook routes, address constraints predicted 2–8 hours ahead. Dispatchers must file flight plans ≥45 minutes before gate push-back; during SWAP they select applicable routes and file revisions. Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) receives operators’ multiple route options and departure-delay preferences but provides no postdeparture optimization. Crews consult controllers/dispatchers for alternate trajectories avoiding weather/flow restrictions and must coordinate with controllers for aircraft-conflict avoidance. Existing automation lacks expired-constraint detection/efficient corrections; manual coordination prolongs diversions.
Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR): NASA-developed/tested ground-based, trajectory-based concept continuously analyzes airborne en route aircraft using weather, airspace and traffic data to propose simple, time/fuel-saving flight-plan amendments accounting for convection, traffic conflicts, sector congestion, special use airspace and FAA routing restrictions. DWR sends route-correction advisories to users, who view/modify routes before requesting/issuing clearance. Its interface strongly warns when modified trial trajectories conflict with forecast weather/traffic. FAA automation implementation is unspecified/generic.
DWR extends NASA’s Direct-To tool (1998–2001); integral Direct-To functionality finds conflict-free, operationally acceptable direct clearances. Direct-To routes meeting user-defined minimum wind-corrected time savings generate advisories regardless of convection. Polygon-based constraint avoidance could address nonweather obstacles, reducing fuel, emissions and controller/pilot workload.
Conditions: fair/adverse weather; SWAP active; no formal modes specified.

New part:
U0050: DWR works by continuously and automatically analyzing in-flight aircraft operating within en route airspace above 10,000 ft to find opportunities for time- and fuel-saving corrections to weather avoidance routes, or simple wind-favorable direct to routes.
U0051: Route corrections are simple route changes like those typically used in today’s operations.
U0052: DWR analyzes and updates trajectories as new radar track and flight plan data are received [2].
U0053: DWR identifies flights that could save a user-defined minimum amount of time (default of five minutes) by short-cutting their current trajectory and returning to the flight plan trajectory via a downstream waypoint on their current flight plan route.
U0054: The DWR flight selection and route correction advisory logic are illustrated in Figures 1 and 2 and summarized as follows.
U0055: All flights at or above 10,000 ft are continuously and automatically analyzed to determine if a direct route trajectory from a Maneuver Start Point (MSP) to a default Return Capture Fix (RCF) could save the user-defined minimum time or more in wind-corrected flight time.
U0056: The MSP is programmable and currently defaults to a point 5 min downstream of present position or to the first point in the high altitude airspace.
U0057: The default RCF for any flight is intended to approximate an operationally acceptable direct route clearance given the location and routing of the flight, the local airspace, and arrival routing limits at the destination airport.
U0058: RCF selection is described in more detail below.
U0059: It is assumed that if a direct route to the RCF, the so-called reference direct route, can save 5 min or more, the flight is likely on some kind of weather avoidance route.
U0060: The reference direct route is then probed for weather and traffic conflicts.
U0061: If weather conflicts are detected, DWR automation inserts one or two auxiliary waypoints as needed in an attempt to identify a minimum delay route around the weather.
U0062: The MSP or any inserted waypoints may optionally be further adjusted automatically to achieve an integrated resolution to weather and traffic conflicts.
U0063: If a solution is found that can save the minimum wind-corrected flight time as defined by the user (5 min default), then a DWR route advisory is posted to an alert list on the user display.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
